reason: The sources document a dramatic Cold War near-miss with 14 well-corroborated claims confirmed across multiple independent news and encyclopedia sites.
story: On September 26, 1983, Cold War tensions were at a boiling point following the Soviet downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007. Just past midnight at the secret Serpukhov-15 bunker outside Moscow, Soviet early-warning computers blared an alarm: the United States had launched five nuclear intercontinental ballistic missiles. Duty officer Stanislav Petrov had less than twenty-five minutes before impact, and military doctrine called for an immediate retaliatory nuclear strike. But Petrov smelled something wrong. If America were truly initiating World War III, an opening strike of only five missiles seemed illogical. Ground radars also showed clear skies beyond the horizon. Trusting his intuition over computer readouts that claimed highest reliability, Petrov reported a false alarm instead of an attack. Later investigations revealed the satellites had mistook a rare alignment of sunlight glinting off high-altitude clouds for rocket flames, narrowly averting accidental Armageddon.
angle: World War III was averted because a Soviet officer realized five incoming missiles made no military sense, exposing that orbital satellites had mistook glinting sunlight on clouds for nuclear launches.

claims.claim: On 26 September 1983, the Soviet satellite early-warning system detected incoming intercontinental ballistic missiles launched from the United States.
Stanislav Petrov was the duty officer on shift monitoring the satellite early-warning system at the Serpukhov-15 bunker outside Moscow.
The early-warning computers first alerted to a single launched missile, followed shortly by alerts for four additional missiles.
The automated computer monitoring system registered the reliability of the missile alert at the highest level.
The incident occurred during extreme Cold War tensions just weeks after the Soviet military shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, killing all 269 people aboard.
Petrov decided against reporting the launch as an incoming attack, instead notifying headquarters that the system had malfunctioned.
Petrov reasoned that a real first strike by the United States would be a massive, overwhelming barrage rather than only five missiles.
Soviet ground-based radar installations capable of spotting missiles over the horizon showed no corroborating evidence of an attack.
The false alarm was caused by a rare alignment where orbital satellites mistook sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds for missile launches.
Military investigators reprimanded Petrov after the incident for failing to record his actions properly in the duty logbook.
The near-miss incident remained hidden from the public until 1998 when retired Soviet general Yuri Votintsev revealed it in his memoirs.
The estimated travel time between the missile launches in the United States and their nuclear detonation on Soviet targets was only 20 to 25 minutes.
Petrov died on 19 May 2017 at age 77, but his passing went unpublicized until months later after a German activist phoned his family.
Petrov was later honored internationally with awards including the Dresden Peace Prize and was the subject of the documentary film The Man Who Saved the World.

disputed: Whether Soviet leadership would have definitely retaliated with nuclear weapons if Petrov had validated the alert: Cold War experts argued the system was on hair-trigger alert to launch, while Russian UN officials and modern scholars assert multiple layers of corroboration and actual detonations on Soviet soil were required before retaliation.
Whether Petrov was forced out of the military following the incident: Western sources frequently claimed he was dismissed, whereas Petrov clarified he took early retirement voluntarily.
Accounts differ on whether Petrov initially notified superiors of a false alarm immediately or waited in silence until the estimated flight time passed without explosions.
